source.text: וַ/יֹּ֣אמֶר לָ/הּ֩ אֶלְקָנָ֨ה אִישָׁ֜/הּ עֲשִׂ֧י הַ/טּ֣וֹב בְּ/עֵינַ֗יִ/ךְ שְׁבִי֙ עַד גָּמְלֵ֣/ךְ אֹת֔/וֹ אַ֛ךְ יָקֵ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה אֶת דְּבָר֑/וֹ וַ/תֵּ֤שֶׁב הָֽ/אִשָּׁה֙ וַ/תֵּ֣ינֶק אֶת בְּנָ֔/הּ עַד גָּמְלָ֖/הּ אֹתֽ/וֹ־־־־׃

translation.text: And Elqanah her husband said to her, “Do what seems good in your eyes. Stay until you have weaned him; only may Yahweh establish his word[a].” So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.

footnotes.text: Or 'confirm' or 'fulfill his word.' The reference of 'his word' is uncertain; one interpretation connects it with Eli's blessing in verse 17. The Hebrew scroll 4QSam-a (4Q51) preserves wording meaning 'what comes out of your mouth,' referring to Hannah's utterance; the Greek Septuagint likewise refers to what came from her mouth. This is a textual variant, not simply another translation of 'his word.' Which reading is earlier remains unresolved.

lexical_decisions.rationale: In context אִישׁ with the pronominal suffix refers to Hannah's marital relation to Elqanah, so 'her husband' is the natural and precise English rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Do what seems good in your eyes
alternatives: Do what is good in your eyes
Do what you think is best
lexical_decisions.rationale: This idiom literally means 'do the good in your eyes,' expressing personal judgment or what appears best to someone. 'Seems good in your eyes' preserves the Hebrew idiom while remaining readable.
The imperative from ישׁב here means to remain where she is rather than to sit physically. 'Stay' is idiomatic modern English.

lexical_decisions.source_word: עַד גָּמְלֵךְ אֹתוֹ / עַד גָּמְלָהּ אֹתוֹ
lexical_decisions.chosen: until you have weaned him / until she had weaned him
alternatives: until you have dealt fully with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this child-nurture context גמל clearly refers to weaning a child, not the broader senses of dealing out or repaying. Using 'weaned' keeps the maternal context explicit.
אַךְ here marks a limitation or qualification to the preceding permission. 'Only' best captures that discourse function.

The jussive nuance fits Elqanah's wish or prayer: 'may the LORD establish.' 'Establish' reflects the causative sense of קום in relation to a word or promise, while leaving open whether the emphasis is confirmation or fulfillment.

Per doctrine, the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה is rendered 'Yahweh' — the transliteration of the divine name — rather than the traditional 'the LORD' substitution. This preserves the personal name God revealed to Israel rather than substituting a title.

The retained WLC reads 'his word.' A connection to Eli's blessing in 1:17 is possible, but not explicit. Published 4Q51 and the Greek instead refer to what comes from Hannah's mouth; that is different source wording, not another gloss of דברו. Preserve the current English provisionally and disclose the variant without deciding historical priority. The historical HALOT label is retained; no fresh lexicon consultation is claimed.
The verb denotes nursing a child. 'Nursed' is clear, natural English without sounding clinical or archaic.
The Hebrew uses the common noun with article, not the proper name. 'The woman' preserves the source wording while remaining understandable in context.

theological_decisions.issue: Reference of 'his word' in Elqanah's statement
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain 'his word' provisionally without identifying a specific divine promise
alternative_readings: what comes out of your mouth (different wording in 4Q51 and Greek)
theological_decisions.rationale: The current WLC wording and the attested alternative refer to different speakers' words. Retaining 'his word' does not decide whether the Qumran/Greek form is earlier. The reader note separates the uncertain referent in the retained text from the source-text variant; no doctrinal or original-text priority is certified.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3 Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it
